placementQuiz.q: Which query finds employees with salary > 50000 AND dept_id = 3?
options: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE salary > 50000, dept_id = 3;
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE salary > 50000 AND dept_id = 3;
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE salary > 50000 OR dept_id = 3;
SELECT * FROM employees HAVING salary > 50000 AND dept_id = 3;
placementQuiz.explain: AND combines conditions; both must be true. Comma is not valid in WHERE.

sections.title: Advanced Filtering — IN, NOT IN, LIKE, BETWEEN

blocks.md: **WHERE is your precision tool. IN for lists, LIKE for patterns, BETWEEN for ranges. Chain with AND/OR — parentheses control precedence.**

blocks.label: IN / NOT IN
blocks.py-pandas:
# IN
e = employees[employees['dept_id'].isin([1, 3, 5])]

# NOT IN
e = employees[~employees['dept_id'].isin([2, 4])]

# Subquery
yc_depts = departments[departments['location'] == 'NYC']['id']
e = employees[employees['dept_id'].isin(yc_depts)]

blocks.label: LIKE patterns
blocks.pg:
-- Case-insensitive
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE name ILIKE 'a%';
blocks.mysql:
-- Case-insensitive (default in MySQL)
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE name LIKE 'a%';
blocks.py-pandas:
# Starts with
e = employees[employees['name'].str.startswith('A')]

# Ends with
e = employees[employees['email'].str.endswith('@company.com')]

# Contains
e = employees[employees['name'].str.contains('son')]

# Regex for single char
e = employees[employees['name'].str.match(r'^J.n$')]
blocks.py-sqlalchemy:
# Starts with
session.query(Employee).filter(Employee.name.like('A%')).all()

# Ends with
session.query(Employee).filter(Employee.email.like('%@company.com')).all()

# Contains
session.query(Employee).filter(Employee.name.like('%son%')).all()

# Case-insensitive
session.query(Employee).filter(Employee.name.ilike('a%')).all()

sections.title: Compound Conditions — AND, OR, NOT, Precedence

blocks.label: boolean logic
blocks.code:
-- AND has higher precedence than OR
-- This: salary > 50000 AND dept = 1 OR dept = 2
-- Means: (salary > 50000 AND dept = 1) OR dept = 2

-- Use parentheses for clarity
SELECT * FROM employees 
WHERE (salary > 50000 AND dept_id = 1) 
   OR (salary > 60000 AND dept_id = 2);

-- NOT
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE NOT (dept_id = 3 OR salary < 30000);
blocks.py-pandas:
# Parentheses for precedence
e = employees[
    ((employees['salary'] > 50000) & (employees['dept_id'] == 1)) |
    ((employees['salary'] > 60000) & (employees['dept_id'] == 2))
]

# NOT
e = employees[~((employees['dept_id'] == 3) | (employees['salary'] < 30000))]
blocks.py-sqlalchemy:
# Parentheses
from sqlalchemy import or_, and_
session.query(Employee).filter(
    or_(
        and_(Employee.salary > 50000, Employee.dept_id == 1),
        and_(Employee.salary > 60000, Employee.dept_id == 2)
    )
).all()

# NOT
session.query(Employee).filter(
    ~or_(Employee.dept_id == 3, Employee.salary < 30000)
).all()

items.q: Because AND binds tighter than OR, the expression A AND B OR C parses as…
items.explain: AND binds tighter than OR. Use parentheses to be explicit.

items.q: Applying De Morgan's law, NOT (A OR B) becomes…
items.explain: De Morgan's law: NOT (A OR B) = NOT A AND NOT B.

blocks.md: EXPLAIN shows how the database *will* execute your query. It reveals: scan type (Seq Scan vs Index Scan), join method, estimated cost, and row counts. At L2, focus on: **Seq Scan = full table read (slow for large tables), Index Scan = targeted lookup (fast)**.
**Cost dropped from 185 → 42. Time from 12ms → 3ms.** Index Scan reads only matching rows; Seq Scan reads entire table. At L3 you'll learn when indexes *don't* help.

items.explain: Sequential Scan = full table scan. Reads all pages sequentially.

options: Index is being used for filtering
items.explain: Index Cond shows the condition applied during index lookup.

blocks.sql: SELECT first_name || ' ' || last_name AS full_name FROM employees;
blocks.pg: SELECT first_name || ' ' || last_name AS full_name FROM employees;
blocks.mysql: SELECT CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name) AS full_name FROM employees;

blocks.md: **ANSI & PostgreSQL use ||. MySQL uses CONCAT().** In MySQL, || is logical OR unless PIPES_AS_CONCAT mode enabled.

glossary.def: Sequential scan — reads every table page; O(N) cost.
Uses B-tree index to jump directly to matching rows; O(log N) + matches.
% (any chars) and _ (one char) in LIKE patterns.
Order of operations: NOT > AND > OR. Parentheses override.
LIMIT n OFFSET m — skip m rows, take n. Page k = OFFSET k*page_size.
Planner's estimated resource units (not milliseconds). Lower = better.
